newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-U.S. Christian television beams message to world.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S. Christian television beams message to world.

text.p: (This is the fourth in a series on the state of Christianity in the United States)
By Alan Elsner
At 8 a.m. every weekday, evangelist Pat Robertson strides to the microphone in the lavish studios of the Christian Broadcasting Network to send his message to America and the world.

That message is not only aimed at spreading the word of the Bible. Robertson sincerely believes that by preaching his brand of religion, he is hastening the end of the world, the return of Jesus and the Day of Judgment.
"I believe there will be two harvests in the years ahead. One is the harvest of grain and the other is the harvest of the grapes of wrath," Robertson wrote in a recent CBN publication.

"Before God's wrath is fully revealed -- and I believe it's coming -- we have quite a job before us. Between now and the year 2000, I believe we will experience the greatest spiritual harvest the world has ever known," he said.

The task of CBN, Robertson says, is to "prepare the world for the Second Coming of Jesus Christ and to establish the everlasting Kingdom of God on earth." He wants to convert 500 million people to Christianity by 2000. To achieve that, he plans to reach 2.5 billion people worldwide.
Robertson told Reuters the end of the Cold War and the collapse of communism was a sign from heaven. "When the Berlin Wall fell, someone in heaven threw a switch," he said.

A former Baptist pastor who ran unsuccessfully for the 1988 Republican presidential nomination, Robertson may have views that sound outlandish to the secular minded. But there is nothing amateurish about the media empire he controls.
REACHES MILLIONS

His daily show, "The 700 Club", named for his first 700 financial backers, went on the air in 1961. It is broadcast on 142 stations in the United States as well as three times a day nationwide on the Family Channel cable network.

The 700 Club is a clever mixture of news, commentary, self-help, inspirational stories, Scripture teachings, prayer and appeals for donations. It claims an average daily viewership of around one million. Three times a year, the network goes all out for contributions in week-long telethons.

"It's very effective political communication. It gives a platform to right-wing spokesman and wraps the message into a nice package," said Matthew Freeman, a senior vice president of People for the American Way, a liberal group which monitors the activities of the Christian right.

The network's 1996 financial statement reveals revenues of over $165 million from donations and an additional $46 million in investment income for a total income of nearly $212 million, compared to $162 million the previous year. The network listed net assets of $256 million.
That is only a small part of the Robertson empire. He also serves as chairman of International Family Inc. which bought the CBN cable network for $600 million in 1990.
He is the power behind the Christian Coalition, a political organisation he founded in 1989 which has become a highly influential voice in the Republican Party.
He is also founder of a right-wing law centre, an international relief organisation and Regent University, a graduate school with a student body of some 1,400.

CBN operates an open prayer line for people to call 24 hours a day which it says has fielded 48 million calls since 1963. And at CBN revivals, miracles are regularly reported. According to CBN publications, the blind see, the deaf hear, the crippled walk and deadly illnesses are cured.
Robertson also recently wrote a novel, "The End of the Age" in which he seeks to expound his views in an easily digestible fictional form.

The plot tells of what happens to the world after a giant meteor engulfs southern California. As society falls apart, the Vice President of the United States is revealed as the Anti-Christ but he is defeated by a small group of believers who band together to form the Christian Resistance Movement.
JESUS IN A SPACE SHIP
Finally, Jesus descends in a giant space craft and lifts the righteous to him in a burst of radiance, while the non-believers burn in eternal hellfire.

CBN president and chief operating officer Michael Little, who is responsible for the network's international activities, says the network is targeting the Arab world, India, China, the former Soviet Union and South East Asia. It is currently broadcasting to around 70 countries in 43 languages.
The network, already the world's largest producer of Arab-language Christian programmes, will soon begin broadcasting to the entire Middle East from an Israeli satellite.
